newsitem.title: UK: Horace Clarkson seeks to buy financial arm.
newsitem.headline: Horace Clarkson seeks to buy financial arm.

text.p: Shipbroker Horace Clarkson Plc said on Tuesday it was continuing efforts to expand into the financial services sector as it reported a dip in profits for 1996.
Managing director Hugh McCoy told Reuters: "It is our ambition to add another division which would cover the broking of financial agreements.
"It is our strong wish to buy a business with the management skills to be able to contribute to Clarksons," he said.
McCoy added that Horace Clarkson had considered a number of acquisitions but had not been able to agree terms. He declined to name target companies.

The London-based group said its core shipbroking business made pre-tax profits of 3.9 million sterling on turnover of 33.4 million stg in 1996 compared with 4.5 million stg on 32.5 million stg turnover in 1995.
Earnings per share increased to 10.8 pence compared with a loss of 26.8 pence per share in 1995 as a result of the disposal of the company's insurance broking division.
The board recommended a final dividend of 2.5 pence per share, giving a total for the year of 4.0 pence against 3.0 in 1995.
Horace Clarkson said: "The fall in profitability was mainly due to development costs in our freight futures broking business and in two of our overseas companies."

Clarksons Securities was authorised to trade in May 1996 while a new office was set up in Beijing by Clarkson Asia. US operations were affected by Horace Clarkson's Stamford-based broking company Seabrokers taking on staff from rival firm Atlantic Chartering with resultant redundancy costs.
McCoy said the overall costs of the restructuring and expansion had amounted to several hundred thousand pounds sterling.

He added that he expected the freight futures and container broking units recently set up would, with an anticipated increased contribution from overseas offices, "help to generate future growth in profits."
The company added that the outlook for shipping markets remained encouraging despite its concern at "the fall in newbuilding prices and the constant threat of overtonnaging."
Horace Clarkson said dry cargo rates fell by an average 34 percent in 1996 from very high levels seen the previous year while tanker rates increased by 23 percent.
McCoy said: "In general our markets balanced each other out with a small net loss."
However, Horace Clarkson added that the shipbroker's role remained under challenge and it expected further rationalisation in the market place.
McCoy said the company was also investigating the possible acquisition of other shipbrokers, but that he regarded many smaller companies as grossly overpriced.
